description: Meet Squadron Zero! We are a group of space geeks and creators from Dhaka, pumped to be part of the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Our crew is a mix of coders, designers, and storytellers, and our goal is simple: take complex open-source data and turn it into something genuinely useful and fun to use. We thrive on teamwork and out-of-the-box thinking. Let's build something awesome together!
summary:
S.H.I.F.T (Satellite Harmonization & Integrated Fire Tracking) turns NASA's fire satellite records into one comparable record from 2003 to today. When NASA FIRMS hotspots from MODIS (1 km pixels) and VIIRS (375 m pixels) are joined end to end, global hotspot counts jump 2.6 times in 2012. That jump comes from the sensor change, not from more fire.

S.H.I.F.T converts MODIS onto the Suomi NPP VIIRS scale with a ratio factor for each 2.5-degree cell and calendar month, fitted on the years both satellites flew. After harmonisation, the 2012 step matches what MODIS alone shows (0.97x against 0.96x). NOAA-20 carries the record forward now that Suomi NPP data production ended on 2 November 2026.

Anyone can open the free website, pick a country, preset, coordinates or a drawn shape, and see a daily and monthly burning-activity calendar, how the latest month compares with its 2003-2025 normal, and the conversion error range. It also shows recent NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 detections and NASA POWER weather as context, and it states its limits openly.

This matters because fire trends, seasons, and unusual months can only be trusted once the satellite change is taken out of the data.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

S.H.I.F.T is a free website and an open data pipeline that turns NASA FIRMS active-fire detections into one comparable global burning-activity record from 2003 to October 2026. Joined end to end, MODIS (1 km pixels, 2000 onward) and VIIRS (375 m pixels, from 2012) records show global hotspot counts jumping 2.6 times in 2012. The planet did not change. The sensor did. S.H.I.F.T removes that jump, so a fire season in 2005 can be compared fairly with one in 2025.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Every FIRMS detection becomes a "hotspot": a 0.05-degree grid cell with fire on a given UTC day. Fire radiative power (FRP) is summed per cell and day. Counting cells instead of raw detections means the finer VIIRS pixels inflate the count much less.

2. Non-vegetation detections and 77,706 cells of persistent non-fire heat (volcanoes, gas flares, industry) are removed in every year.

3. For each 2.5-degree cell and calendar month, a ratio factor (Suomi NPP VIIRS divided by MODIS) is fitted over the years both satellites flew. Where fire is sparse, the factor is pulled toward its 10-degree tile. There is no intercept. Terra and Aqua are merged up to 2019, and Aqua alone is used from 2020, because Terra's orbit has drifted.

4. Before 20 January 2012, the record is MODIS multiplied by its factor. From 2012, it is Suomi NPP, with NOAA-20 filling outage days (including 28 April to 2 June 2026). NOAA-20 matches Suomi NPP closely (1.00 to 1.02 for hotspots, every year 2018 to 2026), so it carries the record forward now that NASA FIRMS stopped producing Suomi NPP data on 2 November 2026.

5. Every rule that could tilt a result was written into a settings file and committed to Git before the run that judged it.

The final record has 51.9 million rows (2002 to 28 October 2026) and is exported as static files for the website.

WHAT THE TESTS SHOW

- The 2012 step after harmonisation is 0.97x, against 0.96x for MODIS alone over the same years (raw join: 2.64x). This shows continuity at the switch. It cannot prove the values before 2012 are right, because the VIIRS-to-MODIS ratio before 2012 cannot be measured.

- Factors fitted on 2016 to 2019 predict the four-year totals of 2012 to 2015 within about 4 percent (fire-weighted median per 2.5-degree cell). Single months are about 18 to 22 percent.

- S.H.I.F.T agrees better with MODIS-alone month classes than simpler corrections (69.3 against 57.6 for the best simple method), it finds 7 of 8 known fire events, and simulated satellite outages are filled within about 2 to 6 percent. These checks are not fully independent, and the Validation page says so beside each result.

WHAT USERS CAN DO ON THE WEBSITE

- Search for a country or preset, type coordinates, or draw any shape on a 2D map or 3D globe (NASA GIBS satellite backdrop, fullscreen mode with a research inspector).

- See "Now against the past": the latest month or any dates compared with the 2003 to 2025 normal for that place, with the ratio, rank, and median.

- Read a daily burning-activity calendar, the fire season, month classes (low, normal, unusual, critical) with cloud flags from MERRA-2, and a monthly trend with conversion error ranges.

- Compare with recent detections: raw NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 VIIRS detections refreshed every 3 hours and kept separate from the historical record.

- See NASA POWER weather for the same dates (rain, humidity, maximum temperature, wind, soil wetness), shown as context, never as a cause.

- Download daily and monthly CSV files, hotspots per 1-degree cell and day, chart images, and a printable one-page brief. Share any view by link.

- Read "The 2012 switch" (raw against harmonised), the Validation dashboard and the Method page, which explain every step, test and limit in plain language.

Two examples from the site: Southeast Australia, September 2019 to February 2020, had 32,583 hotspots, 5.5 times the normal for those months and the highest in 23 years. Bangladesh, 1 to 28 October 2026, had 50 hotspots against a normal of 10, five times the usual and the most in 24 years, outside its normal February to April season (near-real-time data, provisional).

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Fire researchers, land and forest managers, disaster agencies, journalists and students can ask "is this fire activity unusual for this place and season?" over a 24-year record without being misled by a satellite change. It works in any browser and on phones, needs no account or software, and lets you download and trace every number to open code. It is built to keep working as the satellites change: Suomi NPP has ended, Terra and Aqua are drifting, and NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 are the future of the record.

WHY IT IS CREATIVE

Most tools show MODIS and VIIRS as separate products. S.H.I.F.T fits a correction for every place and calendar month, shows an error range for every converted value, fills satellite gaps with tested substitutes, and lets a user see the 2012 jump disappear. It also keeps recent raw detections and weather visibly apart from the harmonised record, so context never becomes a hidden input.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Sensor differences: pixel size, satellite drift, the end of Suomi NPP, and the NOAA-21 data not yet tested against Suomi NPP (shown only in the recent layer).

- Data gaps are shown as gaps, never as days without fire. Cloudy months carry a flag.

- Honest limits: ranges cover conversion error only. July to October 2026 is near-real-time data and provisional. A hotspot is a burning grid cell, not a separate fire. Month classes are statistics, not danger ratings, and areas with very little fire show "Too little fire here to class months reliably".

- Accessibility and reach: works on phones from 320 px wide, keyboard access, colour contrast checked, a dark interface, and static files with no server or API key.

- Security and licensing: the FIRMS key stays in GitHub secrets, map boundaries are used only under open licences, and there are no NASA logos.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

Python (pandas, NumPy, PyArrow, PyYAML, Shapely, h5py, pytest) on Google Colab with Google Drive. React, MapLibre GL JS and Vite for the website. GitHub Actions for tests, the 3-hourly refresh and deployment to GitHub Pages, with a backup copy on Cloudflare Pages. Playwright for browser checks. More than 250 automated tests, plus a fingerprint check that fails if any scientific file changes. Data: NASA FIRMS (MODIS, VIIRS Suomi NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21), NASA POWER, MERRA-2, NASA GIBS, GFED4, Natural Earth and geoBoundaries. AI tools are disclosed in the Use of AI section.
